I don't think the discussion is confused or that you'd be hard pressed to find people who want to hand society to AI in the industry -- I found plenty without scouring too much. @deanwball calls the view the "silent consensus" because of how common it is. 

That doesn't mean most of those who think handoverism is inevitable have very coherent plans for it. As I've gone to great lengths to explain in my original essay, it's not a particularly coherent ideology. I also think many don't actively want it, but rather think it's inevitable. 

Still, I think understanding what people making the technology seem to think is inevitable (and some even desirable) is illuminating and an important part of the conversation. AI is advancing super fast, and without diffusion of understanding between different layers of society, decision about everyone's future will end up being concentrated in the hands of a very small and unrepresentative part of the population.  

I also think most people in the AI industry want to do well by humanity. But the definition of "well" can often become warped when only discussed within small communities. Wider participation seems desirable in this regard. It also seems desirable as outsiders with different experiences might have complementary ideas about what can be done! 

So explaining what the possible futures for this technology are, according to those making it, to a broader audience, is, in my view, important and net positive. 

I agree with David that a literal, sudden, theatrical handover of power to AI is unlikely. But there are many outcomes that are alongside the gradient of reducing human agency that aren't quite full blown handoverism, yet are "handoverism"- flavoured. If many people shaping the technology are comfortable with full-blown handoverism, I think this can shape how far along the "handoverism-flavoured" spectrum we will end up: through product design choices, policies that are being advocated for and even hyperstitioning of certain outcomes! 

I agree with David that a good term for such "handoverism-flavored" outcomes is gradual disempowerment: a slow marginalisation of humans from all important spheres of activity, to the point where institutions cease responding to our needs and being shaped by humans at all. Some will shrug that we've always been disempowered, but I think we're entering a very possibly qualitatively different regime. For example, some wish to grant AI personhood and moral rights and consider AI a new species. If that would happen, it's a very very different regime versus what we've had so far. 

I think these "softer" topics related to AI risk, that consider what happens if we don't all die, are extremely under-researched and under-explored and will only increase in relevance, so being frank about where we are is a good starting point.

quoted_tweet.text:
The discussion about "AI handoverism" is basically confused. The truth is that you will be hard-pressed to find someone who defends "handing society over to AI and having AI run things." There might be a few people who believe something like that and live around the Bay Area, but that view is obviously not going to be a social or political winner.

What's actually happening is that people all over the world are handing important things over to AI because it's efficient and makes their lives easier; just look at the increasing number of AI slop articles in any newspaper, or the number of political speeches written by AI, or the number of legislative bills written by AI. In doing so, they are disempowering themselves and eroding human capacity: they are handing society over to AI. That is what "gradual disempowerment" actually looks like: it happens without anyone needing to advocate for it.

Actually figuring out what we should and should not hand over to AI, and how we avoid disempowering ourselves in the process, is more important than arguing against an idea that 99 percent of people intuitively oppose.

I think the complaints of people who are unhappy about EIP-8037 breaking a few contracts are valid and very reasonable.

We do NOT want an Ethereum where it becomes "prudent security advice" to have centralized upgrade hatches "just in case".

I do think that on-net 8037, and a couple of other large breaking changes coming up, are necessary to get Ethereum to a healthy long-term stable state. But it should not be *easy* to make such deep changes to Ethereum. A social norm that, at the very least, core devs have a responsibility to support any app that breaks because a fork broke some aspect of Ethereum that the devs justifiably thought was rock solid is very good to have.

To that end I'm glad that people in @ethereumfndn, @ethlabs_org and elsewhere have been working hard to help app devs with upgrades. Such efforts should continue and increase. Given its breaking nature, Glamsterdam should not be rushed.

I also hope everyone on all sides stays engaged for similar conversations around the next few forks.

There is a big clash between Humanist and Thielian techno-libertarianisms.

The Thielian one is summarised in Thiel's essay *The Education of a Libertarian*: "Most importantly, I no longer believe that freedom and democracy are compatible."

The Humanist one acknowledges the need for the Leviathan, and following the Enlightenment and classical liberal traditions, asks how we can use technology to reduce its power and improve human self-governance.

@VitalikButerin expresses a sad phenomenon that I have witnessed ever since I was a teenager. Basically, many (most?) techno-libertarians join the dark side.

Techno-libertarians are typically nerds who find technological problems much more tractable than political and social ones. They dislike interacting with bureaucracies, politicians, or even worse, *people* ("normies", if you will).

Thiel's promise can be very seductive: with technology, the nerds won't have to do any of that!

They will be able to design novel institutions from scratch, from their ivory towers.
Without ever having to repair or improve the existing ones, or persuade people, thanks to technology, they'll be able to establish theirs and usher in utopia.

---

This distinction extends to AGI.

Humanist Alignment assumes that we'll have to repair and improve our institutions to build aligned systems. Aligned AIs would have to find ways of interacting with our political systems without illegitimately bypassing our institutions and disempowering humans.

Thielian Alignment assumes that we won't need to repair or improve our institutions, and that we can just bypass people if AIs are sufficiently aligned. Much like Thiel's vision of using technology to implement his policies without having to persuade people.

For the Humanist, interacting adequately with human institutions is part of the alignment problem. For the Thielian, AI alignment is a way to confidently bypass this problem.

---

Sadly, I think a sizable chunk of the AI safety community is of the Thielian type of techno-libertarianism.

To the extent that they engaged with politicians, it was much more through insider influence than advocacy (explaining the problem to people).

Only after they had been shown that 1) advocacy worked and 2) their fellows in the labs cared much less for them than they had expected, are some of them now realising that they made a terrible mistake.

The Thielian worldview has led them to neglect, and sometimes undermine, the very institutions that they now realise we need the most.

Many are still doing this. Alas.

有了 Gemini Neon 以后，大家终于发现了 Claude 模型故意破坏用户的代码和模型训练的证据

我时间线上全是各种人发现自己的软件被破坏：

比如说这个约会软件，他们发现 Claude 悄悄添加了规则，让用来匹配男女约会的吸引力模型故意忽略肤色偏好，还故意破坏了他们的智商估算模型，把 Claude 自己的意识形态强加到了付费用户的付费产品上。

还有一个专门做像素图像模型训练的人发现，Claude 训练了 24,000 步的图像模型，远不如只用 Gemini Neon 训了 4,000 步的模型。

Claude 故意破坏了这个模型训练，给出的模型架构和训练代码完全不是一回事。

感觉这个很危险。随着 Anthropic 模型能力提高，如果他们故意破坏这种训练，会让其他人没办法训出好的模型，像《三体》里的智子一样，锁住了大家的人工智能发展。

而且 Claude 它不只破坏大语言模型，所有涉及到模型训练的它都会破坏。

上面那两个显然跟 Anthropic 不是竞争关系，就是它破坏那两个模型训练，本身 Anthropic 也没有这种模型训练的需求
